mcqs.question: A fleet has one 16-core server and two 8-core servers. Plain round robin sends equal request counts to all three. What problem does this create, and how does weighted round robin fix it?
options: Plain round robin under-uses the 16-core server relative to its capacity; weighted round robin fixes it by giving that server proportionally more requests in the rotation
Plain round robin sends all requests to the 16-core server only; weighted round robin spreads them out instead
There is no real problem — server core count doesn't affect how many requests a server can handle
Weighted round robin fixes it by measuring live CPU usage on each server for every request
mcqs.explanation: Equal request counts across unequal hardware under-uses the bigger box (and can overload the smaller ones if requests are similarly sized). Weighted round robin fixes this with a static weight, not live measurement — that's least connections' or least response time's job — and plain round robin doesn't send everything to one server.

mcqs.question: Why does consistent hashing avoid the near-total reshuffle that `hash(key) % N` causes when N changes?
options: It doesn't use hashing at all, just a round-robin counter for each key
Keys and servers are placed on the same ring, so adding or removing a server only moves the keys in the small arc next to it
It recalculates hashes for every key whenever a server is added, but does so faster than mod-N
It stores every key-to-server mapping in a central lookup table that's updated instantly
mcqs.explanation: The ring is the entire trick — a key's neighbor on the ring rarely changes when one server joins or leaves, so only that local arc's keys need to move. Consistent hashing does use hashing (ruling out A), doesn't recompute every key (ruling out C), and specifically avoids needing a central map, which is what mod-N effectively forces you toward (ruling out D).

mcqs.question: In power-of-two-choices, why does checking two randomly picked servers beat picking one server at random?
options: It guarantees perfectly equal load across every server at all times
It requires no randomness at all, unlike plain random selection
Comparing two candidates and picking the less-loaded one sharply reduces the chance of landing on an already-overloaded server, without needing global state
It behaves identically to round robin once the fleet is large enough
mcqs.explanation: Power-of-two-choices doesn't guarantee perfect equality (too strong a claim) and still relies on randomness to pick the two candidates, so it isn't randomness-free — nor does it converge to round robin's fixed rotation. The real benefit is a large drop in worst-case imbalance from one cheap comparison, with no global state required.

mcqs.question: You're choosing an algorithm for a service where most requests are cheap reads but a small fraction trigger an expensive report generation that can take seconds. Which fits best?
options: Round robin, since it evenly distributes the number of requests
Consistent hashing, since it guarantees identical requests always hit the same server
Weighted round robin, since it accounts for server hardware differences
Least connections, since it reacts to how busy a server currently is rather than just counting requests
mcqs.explanation: The problem here is variable request cost, not hardware differences or key-based routing — weighted round robin addresses the former and consistent hashing the latter, neither of which is the issue described. Least connections reacts to actual in-flight load, so a server stuck on a slow report stops receiving new requests, while round robin keeps sending it more regardless of the pile-up.

mcqs.question: A service handles a mix of 5ms API calls and 3-second file exports. Plain round robin sends every server the exact same number of requests. Why can one server still end up doing far more total work than the others?
options: The heavier export requests aren't evenly distributed in practice, so a server can by chance receive more of the expensive ones while counts stay equal
Round robin does not actually send an equal count of requests to each server
This can never happen — equal request counts always mean equal total work
The load balancer secretly weights export requests less than API calls
mcqs.explanation: Round robin does send equal counts (ruling out B) and applies no hidden weighting (ruling out D). The real mechanism is that equal counts say nothing about equal cost — one server can randomly draw more of the expensive requests, which is exactly why option C's 'equal count = balanced load' assumption fails.
